topic: Delhi HC: an Aadhaar card is not, by itself, proof of date of birth - Aadhaar is mainly proof of identity (UIDAI Office Memorandum dated 20 Dec 2018; Saroj v. IFFCO-Tokio General Insurance (SC) followed); employer who gave ESIC a date of birth of 20 May 1960 in 2010 could not retire a worker on 20 May 2017 relying on an Aadhaar date of 20 May 1959; burden of proving superannuation on management; Labour Court award of back wages till 20 May 2018 upheld, employer's writ dismissed (M/s J. J. Electronics v. Smt. Rosamma Joy, W.P.(C) 16476/2022, Justice Manoj Kumar Ohri, reported 19 Nov 2026)

slides.title: Aadhaar is **not proof** of your birth date
slides.subtitle: An employer could not retire a worker early by relying **only on her Aadhaar card**.
slides.cite: **M/s J. J. Electronics v. Smt. Rosamma Joy** · W.P.(C) 16476/2022 · Justice Manoj Kumar Ohri · reported 19 November 2026

slides.label: What happened
slides.title: Two records, **two birth dates**
bullets: Rosamma Joy says she worked for the firm from **December 1981**, and was removed on **20 May 2017** after asking for revised minimum wages.
The employer said she turned 58 and **retired** that day. It relied on her Aadhaar card, which showed a birth date of **20 May 1959**.
But when she was registered with **ESIC in 2010**, the employer itself had given her birth date as **20 May 1960**.

slides.label: What the Court said
slides.title: Aadhaar proves **who you are**
bullets: Aadhaar is mainly **proof of identity**. By itself, it is **not proof of date of birth**.
A UIDAI office memorandum of **20 December 2018** says birth dates in Aadhaar are recorded from documents or **self-declaration**.
The Court followed the Supreme Court's ruling in **Saroj v. IFFCO-Tokio General Insurance** on the same point.
slides.note: **Law fact:** When records show different ages, courts weigh **which record is more reliable**. They do not simply pick the Aadhaar date.

slides.label: Why the worker won
slides.title: The employer had to **prove it**
bullets: The employer claimed she had retired, so the **burden of proof** was on it. It produced **no document** other than the Aadhaar card.
The ESIC record was made years **before any dispute**. Having recorded 1960 itself, the employer **could not switch** to a different date later.
The Labour Court called the removal **illegal** and gave **full back wages** till 20 May 2018. The High Court **dismissed** the employer's petition.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: Aadhaar is **still valid ID**
bullets: This ruling does **not** make Aadhaar useless. It remains valid **proof of identity**.
It only means the birth date printed on it is **not, on its own**, proof of age when it is disputed.

caption:
Is the birth date on your Aadhaar card proof of your age? Not by itself, says the Delhi High Court 🪪⚖️

Rosamma Joy says she worked for a firm from December 1981 and was removed on 20 May 2017, soon after she asked for revised minimum wages. The employer said she had turned 58 and retired that day, relying only on her Aadhaar card, which showed a birth date of 20 May 1959. But in 2010, when she was registered with ESIC, the employer itself had given her birth date as 20 May 1960.

Justice Manoj Kumar Ohri held that Aadhaar is mainly proof of identity and is not, by itself, proof of date of birth. The Court relied on a UIDAI office memorandum of 20 December 2018, which says birth dates in Aadhaar are recorded from documents or self-declaration, and followed the Supreme Court's ruling in Saroj v. IFFCO-Tokio General Insurance. Since the employer claimed she had retired, it had to prove it, and it produced nothing except the Aadhaar card.

The ESIC record was made years before any dispute, so the employer could not switch to a different date later. The Labour Court's finding that her removal was illegal, with full back wages till 20 May 2018, was upheld and the employer's petition was dismissed. Aadhaar remains valid proof of identity; only its birth date is not conclusive proof of age on its own.

Case: M/s J. J. Electronics v. Smt. Rosamma Joy, W.P.(C) 16476/2022
Court: Delhi High Court, Justice Manoj Kumar Ohri (reported 19 November 2026)
